subject: Art & Design
title: Fitts's Law: Size and Distance Matter for Clicks
description: Learn Fitts's Law: Size and Distance Matter for Clicks in one minute.

hook.text: Apple's dock icons are huge. Submit buttons are wide. Delete buttons are small. That's Fitts's Law in action.

buildup.text: Fitts's Law: the time to reach a target depends on its size and distance. Bigger, closer targets are faster to click.

discovery.text: Screen edges and corners have infinite size (you can't overshoot). That's why menus sit at the top and corners.

twist.text: Mobile design violates Fitts when it puts small tap targets near large ones. Accidental taps frustrate users constantly.

climax.text: Google's Material Design specifies minimum touch targets of 48×48dp.

punchline.text: Make important things big and close. Make dangerous things small and far.

quiz.question: What does Fitts's Law predict about button design?
options: Larger, closer buttons are faster and easier to click or tap
All buttons should be the same size
Button color affects click speed more than size

details.summary: Fitts's Law predicts that the time to reach a target depends on its size and distance — larger targets closer to the cursor are faster to hit. This mathematical principle drives fundamental interface decisions: button sizing, navigation placement, and touch target spacing in mobile design.
details.whyItMatters: Fitts's Law turns button design from aesthetic guesswork into measurable science. Every pixel of size and distance affects usability speed, making it the most quantitatively applicable principle in interface design.
takeaways: Larger, closer targets are faster and easier to hit
The law mathematically predicts target acquisition time
It drives button sizing, spacing, and navigation placement

faq.question: What are the practical implications for button design?
faq.answer: Primary action buttons should be large and prominently placed near the user's natural cursor or thumb position. Destructive actions (delete, cancel) should be smaller and farther away, requiring more deliberate movement. Touch targets on mobile should be at least 44×44 points per Apple's guidelines.

faq.question: How does Fitts's Law apply to screen edges?
faq.answer: Screen edges and corners are effectively infinite-size targets because the cursor stops at the boundary — you can't overshoot. This is why macOS places the menu bar at the top edge and why Windows puts the Start button in the corner. Edge placement makes targets dramatically easier to hit.
